Summary: Jewish burial and mourning customs centre on prompt, honourable burial, mourning that is both bodily and communal, and the tomb as a place of ongoing respect for the dead.
JewishBackground: The dead were buried promptly, usually the same day, washed, anointed with spices, wrapped in linen, and laid in a tomb, often a rock-cut cave like the one Abraham bought for Sarah. In the Second Temple period a second stage became common: after the flesh decayed, the bones were gathered into a small stone box, an ossuary, often inscribed with the name. Mourning was expressed bodily, by tearing garments, wearing sackcloth, and sitting in dust and ashes, and communally: seven days of intense mourning are already recorded for Jacob, and thirty days for Moses and Aaron. The formal seven-day observance later called shiva was systematised in rabbinic Judaism after the Temple period, so its later form should not be read back unchanged into biblical times.
PointsToChrist: EXPLICIT New Testament link: Jesus was buried according to Jewish custom, wrapped in linen with spices by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus and laid in a new rock-cut tomb (John 19:38-42), and Lazarus was raised from a cave tomb with his grave clothes still binding him (John 11:38-44). The burial customs of the Gospels are the customs described here, practised without alteration for the Messiah himself.
Scripture: Genesis 23:19; Genesis 50:10; Deuteronomy 34:8; 2 Samuel 1:11; John 11:38-44; John 19:38-42
RelatedPeople: Joseph of Arimathea; Nicodemus; Lazarus; Mary of Bethany
